functions.name: secure_print
checks: For each byte i in [0, length): calls __ctype_b_loc() and checks if byte is printable (flag 0x4000 = _ISprint). If NOT printable, prints 'You are CHEATER!!!!' and calls exit(-1).
Loop terminates when byte == 0 (NUL) or i >= length.
functions.behavior: Iterates over buf[0..length). For each byte, checks printability via __ctype_b_loc bitmask 0x4000. If printable, outputs via putchar. If non-printable byte encountered, prints error and exit(-1). Stops at NUL byte or when i>=length. After loop, prints 'something goes wrong.'

functions.name: read_input
checks: Loop: i < size, reads one byte at a time via read(0, buf+i, 1).

If i == 0 after loop (no input read): prints 'something goes wrong.' and exit(-1).

memory_operations.description: Write one byte at a time from stdin to buffer
NUL-terminate: replaces last byte (newline position) with NUL

functions.behavior: Reads input byte-by-byte via read(0, buf+i, 1) up to size bytes. Stops on newline (0x0a). If no bytes read, exits. NUL-terminates at position i-1 (replacing the newline).

attack_surfaces.operation: free(data_ptr) then free(struct_ptr) without clearing note_list[index] or decrementing idx
attack_surfaces.reason: After free, note_list[index] still holds the old struct_ptr (dangling pointer). idx is not decremented, so the same index can be selected again. This creates a Use-After-Free condition: view_note can read freed chunk content, and create_note can allocate new chunks that overlap freed ones. Double-free is also possible since the same index can be freed repeatedly (no NULL check on note_list[index] before free).

attack_surfaces.operation: READ: secure_print(data_ptr + offset, length) where data_ptr comes from freed struct
attack_surfaces.reason: If the note at 'index' has been freed (UAF from drop_note), data_ptr at [struct_ptr+0x8] may contain heap metadata (fd/bk pointers). view_note reads offset and length from user, validates against [struct_ptr+0x0] (stored size), then calls secure_print on data_ptr+offset. If struct_ptr itself is freed and reallocated, [struct_ptr+0x0] and [struct_ptr+0x8] are attacker-controlled, enabling arbitrary read (subject to secure_print printable-byte restriction).

attack_surfaces.operation: malloc(0x10) for struct header, malloc(size) for data, then read_input writes user data into data chunk
attack_surfaces.reason: After UAF/double-free, malloc(0x10) or malloc(size) may return a previously freed chunk. If the struct header chunk (0x10) is returned from a tcache bin containing a poisoned fd pointer, the attacker controls [struct+0x0] (size) and [struct+0x8] (data_ptr), which view_note dereferences. This is the write primitive path: writing into the data chunk via read_input can overwrite arbitrary memory if data_ptr was poisoned.

attack_surfaces.input: buf pointer + length (from view_note, ultimately user-controlled via offset/length)
attack_surfaces.operation: READ: iterates buf[0..length), checks printability, outputs via putchar
attack_surfaces.reason: secure_print acts as an information leak channel but with a strict constraint: any non-printable byte (outside isprint mask 0x4000) triggers exit(-1). This limits direct leaking of libc addresses (which contain non-printable bytes like 0x7f). Heap addresses with printable bytes may be leakable. The length parameter is user-controlled, allowing reading beyond intended bounds if the size check in view_note is bypassed via UAF.

attack_surfaces.operation: libc.so.6 resolved from RPATH directory; LD_LIBRARY_PATH takes precedence over RPATH in glibc search order
attack_surfaces.reason: RPATH is set to a specific directory containing the intended libc.so.6 (glibc 2.27). No RUNPATH present. LD_LIBRARY_PATH would take precedence over RPATH, but this is an environmental concern, not a binary vulnerability. The libc is the intended Ubuntu 2.27-3ubuntu1.2 with tcache and no tcache double-free protection.
